q: You are explaining a network where data flows strictly from input to output without loops. What architecture is this?
explain: Feedforward networks pass information in one direction without cycles. Recurrent networks pass data through feedback loops.

q: Your traditional ML model plateaus despite adding millions of new rows. Why are you switching to deep learning?
options: Deep learning performance scales with data
explain: Deep learning models scale in performance as data volume grows. Traditional machine learning models often plateau early.

q: You want your network to learn complex, non-linear boundaries instead of simple straight lines. What must you include?
explain: Activation functions introduce non-linearity into hidden layers. Without them, stacked linear layers collapse into a single linear function.

q: You want an activation function that maps inputs to a strict probability range between 0 and 1. Which do you pick?
explain: Sigmoid compresses inputs into a (0, 1) range, making it ideal for probabilities. Tanh outputs values from -1 to 1.

q: Your network hidden units keep outputting exactly zero for all negative values, stalling half your nodes. What activation is this?
explain: ReLU outputs zero for any negative input value. This can cause neurons to become permanently inactive during training.

q: You are passing an image dataset to a network to extract spatial patterns using moving local windows. What architecture is this?
explain: Convolutional Neural Networks excel at extracting spatial features using localized sliding filters. RNNs are built for sequential data.

q: You need to reduce the spatial size of feature maps in your CNN to lower parameters and memory. What layer do you add?
explain: Pooling layers downsample feature maps by extracting maximum or average values. This reduces spatial dimensions and computation.

q: You are dealing with natural language sentences where words depend on previous words. Which traditional architecture fits this sequential data?
explain: Recurrent Neural Networks process sequential data step-by-step by maintaining an internal memory state across time steps.

q: You are using a pre-trained model on a new, small dataset instead of training from scratch. What is this strategy called?
explain: Transfer learning reuses feature patterns learned on a large dataset to jumpstart training on a new task.

q: You want to compress an input image into a low-dimensional bottle-neck vector and then reconstruct it. What network do you use?
explain: Autoencoders pass data through an encoder bottleneck to compress features, then use a decoder to reconstruct the original input.

q: You want to build a system that takes both an image and a text prompt to produce a caption. What domain is this?
explain: Multimodal AI models process and connect information from different data types, such as text, images, and audio.

q: Your network is processing inputs row-by-row to compute activations and generate predictions. What phase is this?
explain: Forward propagation passes inputs through network layers to generate an output prediction. Backward propagation runs errors backward.

q: You need to update your network weights by calculating gradients of the loss function. What algorithm does this?
explain: Backpropagation computes gradients of the loss function using the chain rule. These gradients dictate how weights are modified.

q: You want a model that learns the underlying data distribution to generate brand new realistic sample faces. What class of model do you need?
explain: Generative models learn data distributions to synthesize new data samples. Discriminative models focus on predicting boundaries between classes.

q: You are sliding a 3x3 grid over an image matrix to calculate element-wise products. What is this grid called?
explain: A filter (or kernel) is a small matrix of weights that slides across an input to extract localized spatial features.

q: You configure your CNN filter to skip two pixels at every step across the image. What hyperparameter are you adjusting?
explain: Stride determines the step size a filter moves across an input matrix. A larger stride reduces output feature dimensions.

q: Your feature map shrinks too fast at the border pixels, causing edge info loss. What technique solves this?
explain: Padding adds extra perimeter rows and columns (usually zeros) around inputs. This preserves dimensions and retains edge information.

q: You need to flatten your 2D feature maps into a 1D vector to feed into a classification output head. What layer do you use?
explain: Fully connected layers map every single input node to every output node. This is standard for final classification heads.

q: You want to look up the mathematical layer space where an autoencoder groups similar compressed features together. What is this space called?
explain: Latent space is the hidden intermediate vector space where compressed representations of input properties are stored.

q: Your network parameters are suddenly updating to NaN during training because gradients doubled at every single layer. What occurred?
explain: Exploding gradients happen when derivatives compound into massive numbers during backpropagation. This breaks weights, causing NaN errors.

q: You want an activation function that fixes the completely dead negative side of ReLU by adding a tiny slope. Which do you pick?
explain: Leaky ReLU allows a small, non-zero gradient when input is negative. This prevents neurons from dying completely.

q: You are optimizing configurations like learning rate, batch size, and dropout rate before training starts. What are these metrics called?
explain: Hyperparameters are settings configured by the developer before training. Model parameters (like weights) are learned during training.

q: You notice your model training slows down drastically at test time because you added a complex step. What layer hurts inference speed?
explain: Dropout should be disabled during inference. Running active dropout masks at test time adds unnecessary random variance and computing overhead.

q: You want to normalize the activations of an intermediate layer across each mini-batch during a training step. What technique is this?
explain: Batch normalization standardizes intermediate layer outputs using the mean and variance calculated across the current training mini-batch.

q: You are implementing a neural network to sort input images into one of 10 completely mutually exclusive classes. Which final activation do you use?
explain: Softmax normalizes the final layer outputs into a mutually exclusive probability distribution that sums to exactly one.
